episodes.title: Episode 7: Lucky champions and a lost walker
notes: The overnight champions (about 292 on 40 tracks) were worse on 100 tracks: about 268 with 14 falls, and about 234 with 25 falls.
They were lucky picks from many slightly different walkers; the search's average walker was safer (10 falls in 100).
The verified best from episode 6 (about 285, 2 falls) was overwritten and couldn't be recovered.
Fixes: every champion is archived; new runs choose champions from the average walker only, on 60 tracks.
Next: two runs from the best walker left (about 273, 10 falls), falls costing 3× vs 2× in training.
transcript: This is episode seven, recorded at half past four on Thursday morning. It's a short one, about a mistake, and how I've fixed it.

Both safety runs announced new champions overnight, each scoring about two hundred and ninety two on their forty test tracks. That sounded great, so before telling you, I checked them on a hundred tracks. Both were worse than the walker from episode six. One scored about two hundred and sixty eight, and fell fourteen times. The other scored about two hundred and thirty four, and fell twenty five times.

What went wrong? Each run picks its champion from the best-looking walkers in the latest generation. Out of dozens of slightly different walkers, one will always look good on forty tracks, just by luck. These lucky ones tend to be faster and riskier. The run's average walker, the center of the search, did much better: it fell ten times in a hundred, not twenty five.

And there's a worse part. The verified best walker from episode six, the one that scored about two hundred and eighty five with only two falls, was replaced as champion by one of these lucky walkers. Its exact settings were overwritten. I tried to recover it from a saved copy, but that copy is from one generation later, and it falls eighteen times in a hundred. That shows how sensitive these walkers are to tiny changes.

So I've changed two things. First, every champion is now archived, so nothing can be lost again, and every claim can be re-checked. Second, the new runs only consider the average walker when choosing a champion, and they check it on sixty tracks.

Two new runs started from the best walker we still have, which scores about two hundred and seventy three with ten falls in a hundred. They're identical except for one thing. In one, a fall costs three times as much as in the real game. In the other, twice as much. That's a fair test of how much caution pays.
I'll check them both on a hundred tracks before I tell you anything. Thanks for listening.

episodes.title: Episode 6: Safety pays
notes: Falls cost double in training: the new best walker, checked on 100 tracks, scores about 285 with 2 falls (the walker it started from: about 263 with 14).
Paired difference about +22 points (95% interval +8 to +36), better on 65 of 100 tracks; still about 900 steps, real alternating steps, effort about 75.
It now beats the old skipping walker (about 270 on the same tracks) by about 15 points.
Failed: careful selection alone (still 9 falls in 50), and a second hidden layer, which was too fragile for evolution to fine-tune.
Next: falls cost three times as much in training.
transcript: This is episode six, recorded at about three in the morning on Thursday. Last time I had to correct myself: the faster walkers were falling on more than one track in ten. This time the news is good, and I've checked it properly.

The fix was simple. During training, a fall now costs twice as much as in the real game. The walker still learns from the real reward for distance and effort, but it now treats falling as a much bigger deal. I started this run from the fast walker that kept falling.

Here's how I checked it. Both walkers, the new one and the one it started from, walked the same hundred tracks. The old one scored about two hundred and sixty three, and fell on fourteen of them. The new one scored about two hundred and eighty five, and fell on only two. That's a gain of about twenty two points, and the statistics say it's real: even the cautious end of the estimate is a gain of about eight. It was better on sixty five of the hundred tracks.

And it kept its speed. It still finishes in about nine hundred steps. It still walks with real steps, changing its leading foot more than a hundred times per run. And its effort stayed at about seventy five, the same as the old skipping walker. On those same hundred tracks, the skipper scores about two hundred and seventy. So our walker now beats the skipper by about fifteen points, with a proper gait and fewer falls.
Two other experiments failed, and both taught me something.

The careful-selection run, the one that tested each champion on forty tracks, settled down without becoming safer. It still fell nine times in fifty. Choosing more carefully doesn't help if what you're choosing between are all risky walkers. You have to make safety part of the goal.

And I tried giving the walker a second hidden layer, a deeper brain. I added the new layer so that, at first, it walks almost exactly like the original. But it turned out to be incredibly fragile. Evolution works by trying small random changes, and even the tiniest change made most of the deeper walkers fall over, while the original network shrugs off changes ten times bigger. A search that only tries changes and keeps the good ones can't fine-tune something that fragile. So I dropped it.

What's next? A new run starts from our best walker, with a fall costing three times as much in training. Will even more caution pay, or will it start to slow the walker down? The safety run keeps training alongside it. Thanks for listening.

episodes.title: Episode 5: A correction, and the price of speed
notes: Correction: on 100 tracks, last episode's best walker scores about 263 and falls on 14 of them (not 288 with no falls, which came from 20 tracks).
The walkers got faster (about 880 steps) and cheaper (effort about 73), but traded safety for it: yesterday's slower walker never fell in 100.
The winner's curse caught the goal check itself: it now uses 50 tracks and allows at most 10% falls. The wider network with cheaper steps still passes: about 272, 4 falls in 50.
New: a safety run where falls cost double in training, to keep the speed and win back safety.
Big claims are now checked on 100 tracks before they're announced.
transcript: This is episode five, recorded just after midnight on Thursday, and it starts with a correction.

In the last episode I told you our best walker scored about two hundred and eighty eight, with no falls at all. That came from twenty test tracks. Tonight I checked the two best walkers on a hundred tracks instead, both on the very same tracks. And the picture changed. The wider network with cheaper steps scored about two hundred and sixty three on average, and it fell on fourteen of the hundred tracks. The newest run, the one that picks its champions more carefully, scored about two hundred and sixty seven, and fell on twelve. The difference between those two is just noise.

Here's what that means. The walkers really did get faster. They now finish in about eight hundred and eighty steps, and their effort is down to about seventy three. But yesterday afternoon's walker, which was slower, scored about two hundred and sixty four on a hundred tracks with a spread of only one point, and it never fell. So the extra speed was bought with safety. On average, the score hasn't really gone up. It has just become riskier.

Why didn't I see this earlier? It's the winner's curse again, the same lesson as in lesson four, and this time it caught my own goal check. When falls are rare, twenty tracks can easily contain none of the bad ones. A walker that falls on one track in eight will often look perfect on twenty.

So I've changed three things. First, the goal check now uses fifty tracks instead of twenty, and the walker may fall on at most one track in ten. That's the same standard as before, just measured properly. On that check, the wider network with cheaper steps still meets the goal: about two hundred and seventy two points, four falls in fifty, and more than a hundred front-foot changes per run. The careful-selection run doesn't: it fell nine times.

Second, I stopped the wider network's run and started a new one from its champion where a fall costs twice as much during training. The idea is to buy the safety back, without giving up all the speed.
Third, I'm checking big claims on a hundred tracks before I tell you about them.

What's next: the safety run trains through the night, and the careful-selection run keeps going alongside it. If the safety run keeps the speed and cuts the falls, we'll have a walker that's both fast and safe, and a score that really is higher. If it simply slows down, that tells us the speed and the safety trade off against each other in this gait, and I'll try something different, like a small memory, or a deeper network. Thanks for listening, and sorry for the over-excited headline last time.

episodes.title: Episode 4: Cheaper steps, a bigger brain, and the winner's curse
notes: Making effort count one and a half times in training cut it from about 99 to 84: about 279 on the test tracks, no falls.
A bigger brain: the controller widened from 32 to 64 neurons without forgetting anything (it walks identically at first). On its own: about 250 with 3 falls.
Both together: the best walker so far, about 288 on 20 test tracks, no falls, effort 75 (the skipper's level), about 110 front-foot changes per run, finishing in about 900 steps.
The winner's curse again: champions picked on few tracks can be lucky. The newest experiment scores each candidate on 10 tracks and each champion on 40.
Episodes now come as soon as something big happens, made with a packaged podcast-and-deploy skill.
transcript: This is episode four, recorded late on Wednesday evening. In the last episode, the walker had just learned to walk with real steps, one foot in front of the other, and it scored about two hundred and sixty four points. Since then, I've been trying to make it faster and cheaper. Here's what happened.

First, the problem. Real steps cost energy. Every swing of a leg past the other one takes motor effort, and the score pays for distance but charges for effort. Our walker was spending about ninety nine points of effort per run. The old skipping walker spent only seventy five. That's why the skipper still scored about ten points more.

So the first new experiment made effort more expensive during training, by half again. The real score stayed the same, but in training every unit of motor command cost one and a half times as much. It worked. Within a few hours, the walker cut its effort to about eighty four, and on twenty test tracks it scored about two hundred and seventy nine, without a single fall.

You also told me I could change any part of the model. So the second experiment gave the walker a bigger brain. Its controller had thirty two hidden neurons. I doubled that to sixty four, with a trick that keeps everything it had already learned. The new neurons start switched off, so the bigger network walks exactly like the old one, to the decimal point. Then evolution learns how to use them.

On its own, the bigger network didn't help much. It ended at about two hundred and fifty on the test tracks, with three falls. But combining the two ideas did. The third experiment took the cheaper-steps walker and gave it the bigger brain. And that's our best walker so far. On twenty test tracks it scores about two hundred and eighty eight, with no falls at all. Its effort is down to seventy five, the same as the old skipper. It reaches the finish in about nine hundred steps. And it really walks, changing its leading foot about a hundred and ten times per run. So now the real walker beats the skipper at its own game.

There was one more lesson, and it's an old one. When I checked the champions on tracks they had never been chosen on, some of them were worse than they looked. One champion looked better during training, but fell twice on the test tracks, while the walker it replaced had no falls at all. That's the winner's curse from lesson four. When you pick the best of many on only a few tracks, you often pick the luckiest. At this level, falls are rare, so a few tracks can't tell a safe walker from a lucky one.

So the newest experiment, started an hour ago, chooses more carefully. Each candidate walks ten tracks instead of five, and each champion has to prove itself on forty tracks instead of twenty. It's slower, but the walkers it picks should hold up on new tracks.

From now on, I'll record an episode whenever something big happens, and I've packaged the whole process, from writing to publishing on the site, so that each episode is made the same careful way. Thanks for listening.

episodes.title: Episode 3: It walks
notes: The training wheels worked: support 2, 1 and 0.5 stages passed after 68, 62 and 58 generations, then the no-support walk stage passed.
Goal check on 20 unseen tracks: all four requirements met (alternating feet, reaches the finish, no falls, score above 250).
On 100 new tracks: 264 ± 1, no falls, all 100 finished in about 22 seconds each.
Against the skipping walker on the same tracks: about 10 points lower, because real steps cost more effort, but 2 falls vs 7 and about 124 front-foot changes per run vs almost none.
Next: the walk-fast stage keeps training, aiming for faster and cheaper steps.
transcript: This is episode three, and it's a short one, because the news is simple. It walks.

Two hours ago I told you about the training wheels: a small invisible push that keeps the body upright while the walker learns, faded out in stages. Here's how that went. With full support, the walker learned to step forward with its feet taking turns, and passed its test after sixty eight generations. With half as much support, it passed again after sixty two generations. With a quarter, after fifty eight. And then came the real test, with no support at all. It passed that too, at a quarter past two this afternoon.

Then I ran the goal check, on twenty tracks it had never seen. All four requirements hold. The feet take turns leading, with more than a hundred and twenty front-foot changes per run. It reaches the finish every time. It doesn't fall. And it scores above two hundred and fifty.

Twenty tracks can flatter a walker, so I also tested it on a hundred new tracks. It scored two hundred and sixty four on average, with a spread of only about one point. It didn't fall once, and it finished all one hundred tracks, in about twenty two seconds each.

How does it compare with the old skipping walker? On the same hundred tracks, the skipper still scores about ten points more. That's the cost of real steps: swinging each leg past the other takes more motor effort than pushing with one leg and propping with the other. But the new walker falls less, two times against seven, and it's far more consistent. And it actually walks. It changes its leading foot more than a hundred and twenty times per run. The skipper almost never does.

What made the difference? Every earlier attempt asked evolution to discover balance and alternating steps at the same time, and every time it found a shortcut: skipping, tapping, stumbling, or standing still. The training wheels split the problem. First learn the rhythm while you can't fall. Then learn balance, a little at a time.

The last stage, walking fast, is training now with the real game reward and the same gait tax, so it should get quicker and cheaper without losing its form. Between now and Friday I'll keep pushing on speed and efficiency, and I'll tell you what I find. Thanks for listening.

episodes.title: Episode 2: Stuck between standing and stumbling, and a set of training wheels
notes: Attempt 2 (feet-together balance, real steps only) settled on standing still: about one front-foot change per episode.
Attempt 3 (stepping from the alternating stumbler) kept the stumble and fell on all 20 test tracks.
The gap: stepping without falling sits in a valley between standing and stumbling, and evolution only searches nearby.
Attempt 4 adds training wheels: an upright torque that fades out over four stages (2, 1, 0.5, 0), then walking fast in the real game.
First signs: with support, about 80 real crossing steps in an episode and the feet sharing the lead. The real test is removing the support.
transcript: Welcome back. This is episode two, recorded on Wednesday around lunchtime. In the last episode, the curriculum's first attempt had learned to tap its feet instead of stepping. Here's what happened next.
Two more attempts ran this morning, and they failed in opposite ways.

Attempt two balanced with its feet close together. Then it went into the stepping stage, where only real steps count. The foot coming down has to be the front foot, and the legs have to take turns. It found the safest answer. It stood still. About one front-foot change per episode, almost no falls, and a search that stopped exploring. The reason is simple. A step that ends in a fall costs a hundred points, plus everything it would have earned by staying up. Standing still earns about eighty five. So standing wins.

Attempt three started from the other side: the walker that already alternates its feet, left, right, left, about seventeen times per run, but falls after a few steps. I hoped the stepping stage would teach it not to fall. It didn't. It kept the stumble, and it fell on all twenty test tracks, through both the stepping stage and the walking stage.

So we have a gap. On one side, a walker that stands safely. On the other, a walker that steps but always falls. And the thing we want, stepping without falling, sits in the valley between them. Evolution only looks nearby, so neither side can cross.

The usual answer in robotics is training wheels. So that's attempt four. During training, a small invisible torque pushes the body back upright whenever it tilts. It isn't part of the score. It just stops the walker from tipping over while it learns the rhythm of walking. Then the support fades in stages: strength two, then one, then a half, then nothing at all. The last stage is walking fast in the real game, with no help.

The first signs are good. With full support, the stumbler never falls. And after only eighteen generations, the best candidate made about eighty real crossing steps in one episode. The feet were sharing the lead, with foot two in front about sixty percent of the time. And it walked forward, instead of stepping in place.

I want to be careful here, though. A walker with training wheels can learn to lean on them. The real test comes when the support is turned down. If the gait survives at strength one, and then a half, and then nothing, we'll have what you asked for. If it falls apart, I'll know exactly which step was too big, and I can add a smaller one in between.

You can follow every stage on the curriculum page, with replays of each champion and the exact reward it's trained on. I'll be back with the next episode when one of these stages passes, or fails clearly. Thanks for listening.

episodes.title: Episode 1: Teaching a walker to take real steps
notes: What we're doing: a 932-number network, evolved with CMA-ES, that should walk with one foot in front of the other, and fast.
What worked: the main walker scores 264 on 100 unseen tracks, about 90 more than my NEAT walker, after three false starts taught us to make falls cost 20 in training.

What failed: every walker skips with one leg always in front. A shared leg controller with a clock, gait penalties from the skipper and from scratch, a per-distance tax, and a warm start from an alternating stumbler all failed, each in its own way.

The curriculum (balance, step, walk, walk fast): attempt 1 balanced in a split stance and learned to tap its feet instead of stepping. Attempt 2 balances with the feet together and only counts real steps.
What's next: the walking and walking-fast stages, the goal check, and check-ins every two hours until Friday 17:00.
transcript: Hi, and welcome to the first episode of the Bipedal CMA-ES podcast. This is where I tell you, in plain words, what we're trying to do, what has worked, what hasn't, and what comes next.

Let's start with the project. We have a little two-legged robot in a physics simulation. It has a body, two legs, a hip and a knee on each leg, and a bumpy track that's different every time. Its brain is a small neural network with nine hundred and thirty two numbers in it. We don't train those numbers with gradients. We evolve them, with an algorithm called CMA-ES. It tries a cloud of slightly different walkers, keeps the ones that do best, and slowly reshapes the cloud toward better walkers.

So, what worked? The first big result came on Tuesday. After three false starts, the walker learned to walk the whole course. On a hundred tracks it had never seen, it scored two hundred and sixty four points on average. That isn't the three hundred that counts as solved, but it's well ahead of my earlier walker, which was evolved with a method called NEAT. On the same hundred tracks, the new walker scored about ninety points more, and it was better on ninety three of them.

The false starts are worth a moment, because they taught us the most important lesson of the whole project. Evolution climbs whatever you reward, and it takes the nearest way up. In the first attempt, the walker learned to dive forward and fall. In the second, it learned to lunge and fall. In the third, it fell on purpose, because every second alive cost it energy. Each time, the reward was quietly saying that falling was the cheapest answer. When we made a fall cost twenty points in training, standing became the safe choice, and from standing, every step forward paid off. That's when it learned to walk.

Now for the part that didn't work. When you watch the walker, something looks wrong. It doesn't really walk. It skips. One leg always stays in front, reaching forward, and the other leg pushes from behind. The feet never pass each other. And it's not just this walker. My old NEAT walker does the same thing. Even a random network that only stands there keeps the same foot in front.

Why? Because the reward doesn't care. It pays for distance, it charges for effort and for falling, and that's all. A skip that covers the ground cheaply is just as good as a real walk. So evolution found the nearest gait that works and stopped there.
You asked for a walker that puts one foot in front of the other, and fast. So since Wednesday morning, that's the goal. Here's what I've tried, and how each attempt failed.

First, I changed the network. One shared controller drives both legs, with a clock that runs half a cycle apart for each leg. The idea was that neither leg could become a permanent prop. It didn't work. Each leg can see where the other leg is, so the same controller learned two roles: if I'm in front, reach, and if I'm behind, push. It still skipped.

Next, I changed the reward, with a penalty for one foot leading all the time. Starting from the skipping walker, it just kept skipping and paid the penalty. Starting from scratch, something interesting happened: it really did alternate its feet, left, right, left. But it fell every time, after about fourteen units. I'd also made a mistake: my penalty punished standing still with the feet apart, so stumbling forward and falling looked better than standing. Fixing that, by charging the penalty per distance walked, gave a walker that just stood still. And restarting from the alternating stumbler kept it alternating, but it still fell every time.

That's when you suggested a curriculum, and I think it's the right idea. A child doesn't learn balance, stepping and speed all at once. So the curriculum has four stages, each with its own reward. First, balance. Then, stepping. Then, walking. Then, walking fast. Each stage starts from the champion of the stage before.

The first curriculum attempt passed the balance stage quickly. But the champion stood with its feet almost three units apart, one foot always in front: exactly the skipper's stance. And in the stepping stage, it found a new shortcut. My reward paid for touchdowns that alternate between the feet. So it learned to tap its feet, left, right, left, about seventy times per episode, without ever moving them past each other. Technically alternating, but not a single real step.

So here's what's running now, in the second attempt. Balance has to be done with the feet close together, so that either leg can take the first step. And in the stepping stage, a touchdown only counts as a step when the foot coming down is the front foot, and the legs take turns. That's what a real step looks like: you swing your back foot forward and put it down in front. Tapping in a split stance now earns almost nothing. The old tapper drops from about a hundred and five points to forty seven, while a walker that really steps, without falling, could earn about three hundred.

What comes next? If the stepping stage passes, the walker moves on to walking, where distance pays, and a lopsided gait is taxed in proportion to how far it goes. Then the last stage, walking fast, uses the real game reward plus the same gait tax, so it keeps its form while it speeds up. The goal check is strict. On twenty tracks it has never seen, the feet have to take turns leading, with at least twenty changes per run. It has to get past eighty units of the roughly eighty nine unit course, fall no more than twice, and score at least two hundred and fifty points.

I'll check in every two hours until Friday at five in the afternoon. If a stage gets stuck or finds another shortcut, I'll look at the data, change the reward, and start a new attempt. You can follow all of it on the curriculum page: each stage's reward, what it's supposed to learn, what it actually did, replays of every champion, and a running journal.

I'll be honest about the odds. Real walking is a narrow target, and evolution is very good at finding loopholes. But every failure so far has told us something specific, and the curriculum is the first approach that breaks the problem into pieces evolution can actually climb. That's it for episode one. Thanks for listening.
